Shared Interactive Features.Aliases And Shortcuts:
`alias` syntax is identical between Bash and Zsh — one of the few genuinely 100%-shared pieces of syntax covered in this doc.

```bash
alias ll='ls -lah'
alias gs='git status'
alias gc='git commit'
alias gp='git push'
alias ..='cd ..'
alias ...='cd ../..'
alias grep='grep --color=auto'
alias df='df -h'
alias free='free -h'
```

## Listing and removing

```bash
alias              # list every currently defined alias
alias ll             # show just one alias's definition
unalias ll            # remove one
unalias -a              # remove all aliases for this session
```

## Aliases are pure text substitution

An alias is expanded by literally substituting text before the command line is parsed — it has no concept of parameters/arguments the way a function does. This matters the moment you want an alias to use an argument anywhere other than tacked onto the end:

```bash
alias ll='ls -lah'
ll ~/Downloads    # works fine — "ls -lah ~/Downloads", argument just appends after

# but this DOESN'T work as hoped:
alias backup='cp $1 $1.bak'    # $1 is not meaningful in an alias context
```

Once you need an argument to appear anywhere other than the very end, or need any conditional logic, reach for a **function** instead:

```bash
backup() {
    cp "$1" "$1.bak"
}
```

Functions work identically for this purpose in both shells (Bash and Zsh function syntax for simple cases like this is the same), and unlike aliases, they properly handle argument quoting/positions, which matters a lot once filenames can contain spaces.

## Zsh-only alias variants (no Bash equivalent)

Zsh has two additional alias types Bash doesn't have at all:

```zsh
alias -g NUL='> /dev/null 2>&1'    # GLOBAL alias — expands anywhere on the line, not just command position
echo hi NUL                         # → echo hi > /dev/null 2>&1

alias -s txt='$EDITOR'               # SUFFIX alias — running a bare file by its extension
./notes.txt                           # → opens notes.txt in $EDITOR, because of the .txt suffix alias
```

- A normal alias only expands when it's the *first* word of a command. A **global alias** (`-g`) expands anywhere on the line, which is how the common `alias -g L='| less'` trick works (`cat file L` → `cat file | less`).
- A **suffix alias** (`-s`) associates a file extension with a command, so typing a bare filename (which Zsh treats as "execute this path") with `AUTO_CD`-adjacent behavior instead dispatches to the registered program.

## A common set worth adopting (works in both shells)

```bash
alias reload='exec $SHELL -l'         # restart the shell fresh, re-reading all startup files
alias path='echo -e ${PATH//:/\\n}'     # print PATH one entry per line (bash syntax shown; zsh: echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n')
alias please='sudo $(fc -ln -1)'        # zsh: re-run last command with sudo; bash equivalent: alias please='sudo !!'
```

The `PATH`-printing and `please`-style aliases above are two small examples of syntax that *doesn't* port cleanly between the shells even though the alias mechanism itself does — worth testing an alias in the shell you actually wrote it for before assuming it transfers.
Shared Interactive Features.Navigation:
## The basics (identical in both shells)

```bash
cd path/to/dir
cd ..            # up one level
cd -              # toggle back to the previous directory
cd                 # no argument: home directory
cd ~user            # another user's home directory
```

## The directory stack: `pushd`/`popd`/`dirs`

Both shells support the classic directory-stack commands, with identical basic syntax:

```bash
pushd /var/log     # cd there, AND remember where you came from on a stack
pushd /etc
dirs -v              # show the stack, numbered
# 0  /etc
# 1  /var/log
# 2  ~
popd                  # pop the top of the stack, cd back to it
cd -2                   # jump directly to stack entry 2 (works in both shells)
```

**Zsh difference worth knowing**: with `setopt AUTO_PUSHD` (see Zsh In Depth → Options & Globbing), Zsh pushes onto the stack on *every* `cd`, not just ones done via explicit `pushd` — meaning the stack becomes a genuinely useful "recent directories" history without you doing anything differently day to day. Bash has no equivalent auto-push option; you must consciously use `pushd` instead of `cd` in Bash for the stack to be populated.

## `cd` quality-of-life differences

| Behavior | Bash | Zsh |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typing a bare directory name to `cd` into it | Needs `shopt -s autocd` | Needs `setopt AUTO_CD` (same idea, different toggle name) |
| Typo correction on `cd` | `shopt -s cdspell` (directory name typos only) | `setopt CORRECT` (broader — covers command names too, see Zsh Options page) |
| `cd` into a path using an env var without `$` | Not supported | Supported if the var is in `$cdpath`-like context; more commonly just type `$VAR` normally in both shells |
| Substring/partial matching in `cd` | No | Yes, with `setopt AUTO_CD` and Zsh's smarter matching, `cd proj` can match `~/Projects` non-exactly under certain completion styles |

## `CDPATH`: search multiple base directories

Both shells honor `CDPATH`, a colon-separated list of directories `cd` searches when given a relative (non-`./`, non-`../`) name that isn't found relative to the current directory:

```bash
export CDPATH=".:~/Projects:~/Work"
cd myproject    # checks ./myproject, then ~/Projects/myproject, then ~/Work/myproject
```

This is easy to forget exists and genuinely useful for anyone who keeps most work under one or two parent folders — it turns `cd myproject` into something that works from anywhere, not just from inside `~/Projects`.

## Named directories (Zsh-only convenience, no real Bash equivalent)

```zsh
hash -d proj=~/Projects/big-project
cd ~proj             # jumps straight there
echo ~proj/src        # also expands inside paths generally, not just after cd
```

This is distinct from a plain alias or `CDPATH` entry — it creates a genuine `~name` expansion recognized throughout path contexts (including in `%~`-based prompt segments, which will abbreviate a long path back down to `~proj` automatically once registered).

## Fuzzy directory jumping (neither shell natively, but extremely common addition)

Most people navigating large numbers of directories eventually add a third-party tool rather than relying on `CDPATH`/directory-stack alone — `zoxide` (a modern `z`/`autojump` successor) is the most commonly recommended today and integrates as a shell function/`cd` wrapper in both Bash and Zsh identically. Covered in Customization & Ecosystem → Popular Plugins And Tools.
Shared Interactive Features.Environment Variables And PATH:
## Setting and exporting variables

Identical syntax in both shells:

```bash
MY_VAR="hello"           # shell variable — visible only to this shell, not child processes
export MY_VAR              # now it IS passed to child processes (programs you launch from here)
export ANOTHER="value"      # can export and assign in one step

echo $MY_VAR
unset MY_VAR                 # remove it entirely
```

The distinction matters more than people initially expect: a variable that's set-but-not-exported is invisible to, say, a script or program launched from your shell, even though `echo $VAR` inside the shell itself shows it fine — because `echo` is a shell builtin reading the shell's own variable table, not a separate process needing it passed down.

## `PATH`: modifying safely

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"     # prepend — new entries take priority
export PATH="$PATH:/opt/some-tool/bin"     # append — existing entries take priority over this one
```

Order matters: `PATH` is searched left to right, so the *first* matching executable found wins. Prepending is the usual choice for personal tool installs/overrides (you want your version found before the system one); appending suits fallback-only tools.

**Common mistake**: setting `PATH` (rather than extending it) — `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin"` without `:$PATH` on the end wipes out the rest of the system path, meaning even `ls` stops resolving. Always include the existing `$PATH` in the assignment unless you deliberately want a minimal/sandboxed environment.

### Avoiding duplicate `PATH` entries

A `.bashrc`/`.zshrc` that's been edited many times over the years tends to accumulate the same directory prepended repeatedly (e.g. from being sourced multiple times, or copy-pasted config blocks). A small guard avoids this, and works identically in both shells:

```bash
case ":$PATH:" in
    *":$HOME/.local/bin:"*) ;;                          # already present, do nothing
    *) export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ;;
esac
```

Zsh alone also has a cleaner native mechanism via its `path` array (see below) that avoids this problem entirely without a manual guard.

## Zsh's `path` array: same data, nicer interface

Zsh automatically keeps a special array variable `path` in sync with the scalar `$PATH` string — editing either one updates the other. This makes `PATH` manipulation in Zsh noticeably more pleasant than string-splicing:

```zsh
typeset -U path    # keep the array de-duplicated automatically — no more repeat-entry problem, ever
path=($HOME/.local/bin $path)     # prepend, array-style
path+=(/opt/some-tool/bin)          # append, array-style

echo $path            # still just a normal-looking PATH string when printed as a scalar
```

`typeset -U` ("unique") is the key piece — once set, Zsh silently drops duplicate entries any time the array is modified, permanently solving the duplicate-`PATH`-entry problem that Bash needs a manual `case` guard for. This has no direct Bash equivalent since Bash's `PATH` is a plain string with no parallel array representation.

## Where to put this, per shell

Cross-referencing Getting Started → Startup Files: environment variables and `PATH` should generally go in the files read once per **login**, not the interactive-only rc files, so that non-interactive child processes (cron jobs, GUI apps launched from a login-session `PATH`, etc.) see them too:

```
Bash:  ~/.bash_profile  (or ~/.profile — see Startup Files page for the tradeoffs)
Zsh:   ~/.zshenv or ~/.zprofile
```

Putting `export PATH=...` only in `~/.bashrc`/`~/.zshrc` is a common beginner mistake that "works" for everyday terminal use but breaks the moment something needs `PATH` without going through an interactive shell first (a surprisingly common source of "works in my terminal but not when double-clicked from the file manager" bugs).

## `EDITOR` / `VISUAL`: worth setting explicitly

Many tools (`git commit` with no `-m`, `crontab -e`, `fc` in Zsh, `edit-command-line` in Zsh's ZLE) fall back to `$EDITOR`/`$VISUAL` when they need to open an editor. Left unset, behavior varies by distro/tool (sometimes `vi`, sometimes a failure). Setting both explicitly avoids surprises:

```bash
export EDITOR="nvim"
export VISUAL="$EDITOR"
```

`VISUAL` is technically for full-screen editors and `EDITOR` for line editors historically, but in practice almost nothing distinguishes them anymore — setting both to the same value is the standard modern convention.
Shared Interactive Features.Job Control Basics:
The core job-control model — suspend, background, foreground, and the signals involved — is POSIX-derived and works identically in both shells at the everyday-usage level. This page is deliberately short; it covers only what's genuinely identical. Bash-specific edge cases (`disown`, `nohup` interplay) live on Bash In Depth → Job Control & Options, since Zsh's equivalents, while similar, have some differing defaults covered there separately if relevant.

## Identical core commands

```bash
command &      # start in background
Ctrl-Z           # suspend current foreground job
jobs              # list jobs
fg                 # foreground the most recent job
fg %2                # foreground job 2 specifically
bg                    # background the most recent suspended job
bg %2                   # background job 2 specifically
kill %1                   # signal a job by job number, not PID
wait                        # wait for all background jobs to finish
wait %2                       # wait for one specific job
```

## Identical job reference syntax

```
%1     job number 1
%%      the current job
%+       same as %% (current job)
%-        the previous job
%git       most recent job whose command line starts with "git"
%?compile   most recent job whose command line CONTAINS "compile" anywhere
```

## Where the shells genuinely differ (see each shell's own page for detail)

- **Job-exit notification timing** — Zsh by default reports a background job's completion status more eagerly (can interrupt your prompt line to tell you), while Bash waits until just before drawing the next prompt. Both are configurable (`setopt NOTIFY` in Zsh turns on immediate notification; it's Zsh's default already in most builds).
- **`disown` and `nohup` semantics** — covered fully on Bash's page; Zsh supports the same `disown` builtin with the same core behavior, but interacts slightly differently with `setopt HUP`/`NO_HUP` (whether background jobs get `SIGHUP` on shell exit at all, which Zsh can control directly as an option rather than requiring the external `nohup` command as a workaround).

## Why you'll reach for a multiplexer instead, eventually

Job control is genuinely useful for short-lived background tasks within a single terminal session, but it doesn't survive the terminal window closing, doesn't give you multiple independent scrollback buffers, and doesn't let you reattach from a different physical machine. Once those matter, a terminal multiplexer (tmux/screen) is the natural next tool — see Shared Interactive Features → Terminal Multiplexers.
Shared Interactive Features.Terminal Multiplexers:
A terminal multiplexer runs *outside* your shell (technically: your shell runs *inside* it, as one or more panes), and neither Bash nor Zsh has any built-in awareness of it — but the two are used together constantly, and a few interactions are worth knowing since they affect how your shell config behaves.

## tmux vs screen

```bash
# Arch:
sudo pacman -S tmux
# screen is available too, but tmux has been the more common default for years:
sudo pacman -S screen
```

Both let you: split a terminal into multiple panes, create multiple named sessions, detach from a session (leaving programs running) and reattach later — including from a different SSH connection or after closing your terminal emulator entirely. tmux is generally considered to have a more modern config format, better default splitting UX, and wider plugin ecosystem today; screen is older and more minimal but still shows up on systems where installing tmux isn't an option.

## Minimal tmux config (`~/.tmux.conf`)

```
# more intuitive prefix (default is Ctrl-b, many prefer Ctrl-a like screen)
set -g prefix C-a
unbind C-b
bind C-a send-prefix

# sane split bindings
bind | split-window -h
bind - split-window -v

# mouse support (scrolling, pane resize, pane select)
set -g mouse on

# true color support, matters for prompt themes / syntax highlighting inside panes
set -g default-terminal "tmux-256color"
set -ag terminal-overrides ",xterm-256color:RGB"
```

## Why each new pane starts a fresh shell — and why that's usually fine

Every new tmux/screen pane launches a brand-new shell process, which means your full startup-file chain runs again per pane (see Getting Started → Startup Files for exactly which files, depending on whether tmux launches panes as login or non-login shells — configurable via tmux's own `default-command`/login-shell setting). This is rarely a problem in practice since `.bashrc`/`.zshrc` are meant to be fast and idempotent, but it does mean:

- Any slow operation in your rc file (a network call, a large `eval $(...)`, an uncached `compinit`) is paid on *every pane*, not just once per terminal window — this is one of the more common reasons people notice and go fix Zsh's `compinit` caching (see Zsh In Depth → Completion System) after adopting tmux heavily.
- Shell-level state (aliases, functions, exported variables set interactively rather than in an rc file) does **not** carry over to a new pane, since it's a genuinely separate process — only what's written into a startup file persists across panes.

## `SHARE_HISTORY` / the Bash shared-history trick pair naturally with panes

Since multiple simultaneous shells (one per pane) is exactly the scenario Zsh's `SHARE_HISTORY` (see Zsh In Depth → History) and Bash's `PROMPT_COMMAND`-based shared-history trick (see Bash In Depth → History) were designed for, people who use tmux heavily tend to notice and value this feature more than people who mostly use a single terminal window — it's the difference between a command typed in pane 1 being immediately recallable via `Ctrl-R` in pane 2, versus not.

## Status bar and prompt overlap

tmux has its own status bar (bottom of screen, showing window/pane list, and whatever else you configure — clock, battery, etc.) which is a *separate* system from your shell's `PS1`/`PROMPT`. They don't conflict, but it's worth knowing tmux's status bar can duplicate information (like a clock, or git branch via a tmux plugin) that a shell prompt framework like Starship also shows — most people pick one place to show a given piece of info rather than both, purely for visual de-cluttering.

## Nested sessions

Running tmux inside tmux (e.g. tmux locally, SSH into a remote box, tmux again there) works, but both layers respond to the same prefix key by default, requiring either a different prefix for the inner session or pressing the prefix twice (`C-a C-a`) to pass it through to the nested one. This is a tmux-configuration concern rather than a shell one, but it's a common point of confusion for people newly combining SSH + tmux + a customized shell prompt, since a broken-looking prompt after SSHing into a nested session is very often actually a tmux pass-through issue, not a shell config issue.

Everything in Getting Started, Bash In Depth, Zsh In Depth, and Shared Interactive Features is achievable with the shells' own built-in mechanisms and no third-party software. This section covers the ecosystem people typically layer on top: frameworks that manage plugins and config for you, individual popular plugins/tools worth knowing about regardless of framework, prompt frameworks that work across both shells, and fonts/terminal considerations that affect how all of the above actually looks.

Pages in this section:

- **Prompt Frameworks** — Starship (cross-shell), Powerlevel10k (Zsh-specific), and how they relate to the raw `PS1`/`PROMPT` mechanisms covered earlier.
- **Popular Plugins And Tools** — syntax highlighting, autosuggestions, fzf integration, zoxide, direnv — the small set of additions that show up in nearly everyone's setup regardless of which framework (if any) they use.

## A framework is optional, not required

Everything a framework like Oh My Zsh gives you is, under the hood, just `.zshrc` content — `setopt` calls, `bindkey` calls, sourced plugin scripts, a `PROMPT` assignment. Reading the earlier sections of this doc is enough to hand-roll an equivalent setup, and plenty of experienced users do exactly that, valuing the faster startup time and full understanding of every line over a framework's convenience. Frameworks earn their keep mainly by bundling curated defaults and making plugin discovery/updates trivial — a real convenience, but a tradeoff (startup latency, opacity, occasional plugin-conflict debugging) rather than a strict improvement in every case.
Customization & Ecosystem.Shell Frameworks:
## Oh My Zsh

The most widely known Zsh framework — a large bundled collection of plugins and themes, installed via a curl-pipe-to-shell script that clones itself into `~/.oh-my-zsh` and adds a block to `~/.zshrc`.

```bash
sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)"
```

```zsh
# ~/.zshrc, after installation
export ZSH="$HOME/.oh-my-zsh"
ZSH_THEME="robbyrussell"
plugins=(git docker fzf z)
source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh
```

- **What it actually does**: sources a large init script that sets a bunch of sane `setopt`s, defines helper functions, loads whichever plugins you listed (each plugin is just a directory with a `.plugin.zsh` file that gets sourced), and applies a theme (which is just a `PROMPT`/`RPROMPT` assignment, same mechanism covered in Zsh In Depth → Prompt).
- **Tradeoffs**: huge plugin/theme ecosystem and by far the most tutorials/community support of any option here, at the cost of being one of the slower frameworks to start up if you enable many plugins, and being fairly opinionated/opaque about what it changes under the hood unless you go read the source.

## Prezto

An older, generally faster alternative to Oh My Zsh with a more modular "modules" concept instead of loose plugins, and more conservative/POSIX-minded defaults.

```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/sorin-ionescu/prezto.git "${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zprezto"
```

Configuration lives in `~/.zpreztorc`, listing enabled modules (`git`, `history`, `completion`, `prompt`, etc.) rather than Oh My Zsh's flat plugin-name array — a marginally more structured approach that some people prefer for larger configs.

## Zinit / Zap: modern lightweight Zsh plugin managers

A newer generation of Zsh plugin managers exists specifically to address Oh My Zsh's startup-time cost, by supporting **lazy-loading** (a plugin's code doesn't actually execute until the command it provides is first used) and **turbo mode** (deferring plugin loading until after the prompt is already interactive, so you can start typing before every plugin has finished loading):

```zsh
# Zinit, minimal example
zinit light zsh-users/zsh-autosuggestions
zinit light zsh-users/zsh-syntax-highlighting
zinit snippet OMZP::git   # even lets you cherry-pick individual Oh My Zsh plugins without the whole framework
```

These don't come with a curated theme/plugin bundle the way Oh My Zsh does — you're expected to assemble your own list — which suits people who've already decided which 5-10 plugins they actually want rather than starting from a big default set.

## bash-it: Bash's rough equivalent

Bash's ecosystem is considerably smaller than Zsh's (a natural consequence of Bash's more limited native extensibility — no `zstyle`, no widget system, no `compsys`), but `bash-it` fills a similar role: bundled themes, plugins (mostly aliases + completion glue), and a management CLI.

```bash
git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/Bash-it/bash-it.git ~/.bash_it
~/.bash_it/install.sh
bash-it enable plugin git
bash-it enable completion git
bash-it show themes
```

It's meaningfully less powerful than the Zsh frameworks above simply because Bash itself has less to hook into — there's no Bash equivalent of Zsh's widget system or `compsys` styles for a framework to build rich behavior on top of, so `bash-it`'s plugins tend to be simpler (mostly alias sets and `PS1` themes) than Zsh plugins.

## Should you use one at all?

A reasonable decision framework:

- **New to either shell, want to see good defaults quickly** → Oh My Zsh (Zsh) or bash-it (Bash) is a fine on-ramp; you can always strip it back out once you understand what you actually use.
- **Care about startup latency, comfortable assembling your own config** → Zinit/Zap (Zsh) or hand-rolled `.bashrc` (Bash — there isn't a strong lightweight-manager equivalent, but Bash's smaller surface area makes hand-rolling less work than in Zsh anyway).
- **Want maximum understanding of every line running in your shell** → skip frameworks entirely, use this doc's Bash/Zsh In Depth sections directly plus the individual plugins from Popular Plugins And Tools, sourced by hand.

None of these are mutually exclusive with using Starship for the prompt specifically — see Prompt Frameworks, next.
Customization & Ecosystem.Prompt Frameworks:
Where Shell Frameworks (Oh My Zsh, Prezto, bash-it) bundle plugins *and* a theme together, prompt frameworks do one job — the prompt — but do it across shells and with more polish (async rendering, consistent icons, smart truncation) than most people want to hand-roll from raw `PS1`/`PROMPT` escapes.

## Starship: cross-shell, the most commonly recommended today

Starship is a single compiled binary (Rust) that generates prompt output and hands it to whichever shell you're in — it works identically whether you're using Bash, Zsh, Fish, or others, which is its main selling point over shell-specific options.

```bash
# Arch:
sudo pacman -S starship
```

```bash
# ~/.bashrc — last line
eval "$(starship init bash)"
```

```zsh
# ~/.zshrc — last line
eval "$(starship init zsh)"
```

Configuration is a single TOML file, shared across both shells if you use both:

```toml
# ~/.config/starship.toml
format = """
$directory$git_branch$git_status
$character"""

[directory]
truncation_length = 3
style = "blue bold"

[git_branch]
symbol = " "

[character]
success_symbol = "[➜](bold green)"
error_symbol = "[➜](bold red)"
```

Starship renders "modules" (directory, git branch/status, language version indicators, command duration, exit code, etc.) largely asynchronously, which is why a Starship prompt in a slow/large git repo generally doesn't block you from typing the way a naive hand-rolled `$(__git_ps1)`/`vcs_info` call can.

Because the *same* config file drives both shells, Starship is a common choice specifically for people who move between Bash and Zsh (e.g. Bash on a minimal server, Zsh locally) and want visual consistency without maintaining two separate prompt configs.

## Powerlevel10k: Zsh-specific, historically the fastest

Powerlevel10k is a Zsh **theme** (works as a plugin within Oh My Zsh/Prezto/Zinit, or standalone) rather than a cross-shell binary. It's historically been the go-to choice for people who want an extremely fast, highly configurable, icon-rich prompt and don't need Bash compatibility.

```zsh
# as a standalone Zsh plugin, e.g. with Zinit:
zinit ice depth=1
zinit light romkatv/powerlevel10k
```

```zsh
# ~/.zshrc
[[ ! -f ~/.p10k.zsh ]] || source ~/.p10k.zsh
```

Its defining feature is `p10k configure`, an interactive wizard run once that asks visual questions ("which of these looks best?") and writes out a complete `~/.p10k.zsh` config file for you — a notably more approachable customization path than hand-editing TOML/`PROMPT` escapes, at the cost of being Zsh-only.

## Comparing the two

| | Starship | Powerlevel10k |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shell support | Bash, Zsh, Fish, others | Zsh only |
| Config format | TOML | Zsh script (`~/.p10k.zsh`), generated by a wizard |
| Setup style | Hand-edit config, or copy a preset | Interactive `p10k configure` wizard |
| Async rendering | Yes | Yes |
| Distribution | Single compiled binary | Zsh script/plugin, needs a plugin manager or manual clone |

## Both need a Nerd Font to look right

Neither renders correctly without a font that includes the glyph ranges they use for icons (git branch symbol, folder icons, OS logos, etc.) — see Customization & Ecosystem → Fonts And Icons. Without one, you'll see boxes or `?` characters in place of icons; this is a terminal-emulator/font configuration issue, not a bug in either tool or in your shell config.

## Going back to raw `PS1`/`PROMPT`

Nothing about adopting Starship or Powerlevel10k is irreversible or exclusive — both simply overwrite `PROMPT`/`PS1` at shell startup (Starship via its `eval "$(starship init ...)"` line, P10k via its theme file), so removing the relevant line from your rc file and falling back to a manually-set `PS1`/`PROMPT` (as covered in Bash In Depth → Prompt and Zsh In Depth → Prompt) always works.
Customization & Ecosystem.Popular Plugins And Tools:
A small set of additions shows up in nearly every serious Bash/Zsh setup, independent of which framework (if any) is otherwise in use. This page covers the ones worth knowing regardless of your framework choice.

## Syntax highlighting

Colors commands as you type — valid commands green, invalid ones red, strings/paths distinctly colored — entirely at the line-editing layer, before you've even pressed Enter.

**Zsh** (`zsh-syntax-highlighting`, must be sourced *last* in your rc file, after other plugins that define widgets):

```bash
sudo pacman -S zsh-syntax-highlighting
```
```zsh
# ~/.zshrc — near the very end
source /usr/share/zsh/plugins/zsh-syntax-highlighting/zsh-syntax-highlighting.zsh
```

**Bash** has no true equivalent — readline has no per-character live-highlighting hook the way ZLE's widget system does, which is a genuine capability gap rather than a missing package. This is one of the more commonly cited concrete reasons people prefer Zsh's editing experience specifically.

## Autosuggestions

As you type, shows a dim inline suggestion completing your command based on history — press `→` (End-of-line key) to accept it.

**Zsh** (`zsh-autosuggestions`):

```bash
sudo pacman -S zsh-autosuggestions
```
```zsh
source /usr/share/zsh/plugins/zsh-autosuggestions/zsh-autosuggestions.zsh
bindkey '^ ' autosuggest-accept   # optional: Ctrl-Space to accept instead of only End/Right-arrow
```

**Bash** doesn't have a natural equivalent either, for the same underlying reason (no live-rendering hook), though tools like `fzf`'s `Ctrl-R` (below) partially cover the same underlying need — fast recall of a previously-run similar command — via a different interaction style (an explicit search popup rather than inline ghost text).

## fzf: fuzzy finder, integrates with both shells identically

`fzf` is a general-purpose fuzzy finder that most people first encounter through its shell integration: a dramatically better `Ctrl-R` (history search) and `Ctrl-T` (fuzzy file finder, inserts the picked path onto your command line), plus `**<Tab>` fuzzy completion.

```bash
sudo pacman -S fzf
```

```bash
# ~/.bashrc
source /usr/share/fzf/key-bindings.bash
source /usr/share/fzf/completion.bash
```

```zsh
# ~/.zshrc
source /usr/share/fzf/key-bindings.zsh
source /usr/share/fzf/completion.zsh
```

Once sourced, `Ctrl-R` in either shell opens a fuzzy-searchable, live-preview history picker instead of readline's/ZLE's built-in linear incremental search — genuinely one of the highest-value-per-minute-invested additions for either shell.

## zoxide: smarter `cd`

A `cd` replacement that learns which directories you visit most (frecency-based, like browser address-bar ranking: frequency + recency) and lets you jump with a fuzzy partial name instead of a full path.

```bash
sudo pacman -S zoxide
```

```bash
# ~/.bashrc
eval "$(zoxide init bash)"
```
```zsh
# ~/.zshrc
eval "$(zoxide init zsh)"
```

```bash
z proj          # jumps to the highest-ranked directory matching "proj", e.g. ~/Work/big-project
zi proj          # interactive picker when there are multiple close matches
```

Works identically in both shells since it's implemented as a shell function generated by the same `zoxide init` command, just targeting different shell syntax under the hood.

## direnv: per-directory environment variables

Automatically loads/unloads environment variables (and can modify `PATH`) when you `cd` into (and out of) a directory containing a `.envrc` file — common for per-project tool versions, API keys for local dev, etc.

```bash
sudo pacman -S direnv
```

```bash
# ~/.bashrc
eval "$(direnv hook bash)"
```
```zsh
# ~/.zshrc
eval "$(direnv hook zsh)"
```

```bash
# in a project directory:
echo 'export API_KEY=local-dev-key' > .envrc
direnv allow    # required once per .envrc, as a safety measure against auto-executing untrusted code
```

The explicit `direnv allow` step exists specifically so that `cd`-ing into a directory you don't control (e.g. a freshly cloned repo) doesn't silently execute arbitrary shell code from its `.envrc` — worth understanding rather than reflexively running `direnv allow` on autopilot.

## A reasonable "just these four" starter set

For someone not adopting a full framework, `zsh-syntax-highlighting` + `zsh-autosuggestions` + `fzf` + `zoxide` (with Bash swapping out the first two, which don't apply) covers the vast majority of what people actually notice and value from a "someone's Zsh setup feels so much nicer than mine" comparison — well before reaching for a whole framework.
Customization & Ecosystem.Fonts And Icons:
This page is included because it's the single most common source of "I followed the tutorial exactly and my prompt looks broken" confusion — and the fix lives entirely outside the shell, in font/terminal configuration, which is easy to not think to check.

## Why prompt themes need special fonts

Starship, Powerlevel10k, and most Oh My Zsh themes use glyphs for git branches (`\ue0a0`-style), folders, OS logos, and separator/"powerline" arrows (``) that are **not** part of standard Unicode ranges any normal font ships. These come from icon sets (Font Awesome, Devicons, Powerline symbols, Material Design Icons, and others) that have been merged into patched font files collectively distributed as **Nerd Fonts**.

Without a Nerd Font installed and actually selected in your terminal emulator, these glyphs render as empty boxes (`▯`), question marks in a box, or get silently dropped — this is expected behavior for a font that doesn't contain the needed code points, not a bug in the shell or prompt tool.

## Installing a Nerd Font on Arch

```bash
# a few common choices, all packaged:
sudo pacman -S ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd
sudo pacman -S ttf-firacode-nerd
sudo pacman -S ttf-hack-nerd
# or browse the full set:
pacman -Ss nerd-fonts
```

(AUR also has `nerd-fonts-complete`/individual `-git` packages if a specific one you want isn't in the official `nerd-fonts` package split yet.)

## Selecting it in your terminal emulator

This step is **per terminal emulator**, not global, and not something Bash/Zsh config controls at all:

- **Alacritty** — `~/.config/alacritty/alacritty.toml`: `[font.normal] family = "JetBrainsMono Nerd Font"`
- **kitty** — `~/.config/kitty/kitty.conf`: `font_family JetBrainsMono Nerd Font`
- **GNOME Terminal / most GTK terminals** — Preferences → Profile → Text → Custom Font
- **WezTerm** — `~/.wezterm.lua`: `config.font = wezterm.font("JetBrainsMono Nerd Font")`

After changing this, fully restart the terminal emulator (not just open a new tab/window in some cases, depending on the emulator) for the font change to take effect.

## True color (24-bit) support

Separately from icon glyphs, many themes use smooth 24-bit RGB colors rather than the older 256-color palette. Most modern terminal emulators support this by default; verify with:

```bash
printf "\x1b[38;2;255;100;0mTRUECOLOR TEST\x1b[0m\n"
```

If that prints a specific orange rather than an approximated palette color, true color is working. If not, check `$TERM` (should generally be `xterm-256color` or better, ideally something indicating truecolor support like tmux's `tmux-256color` when inside tmux — see Shared Interactive Features → Terminal Multiplexers for the tmux-specific setting) and your terminal emulator's own color documentation.

## Quick diagnostic checklist

When a prompt theme looks broken, check in this order before suspecting the shell config at all:

1. Is a Nerd Font actually installed? (`fc-list | grep -i nerd`)
2. Is it actually *selected* in the terminal emulator's font setting (not just installed on the system)?
3. Did the terminal emulator get fully restarted after the font change?
4. If inside tmux/screen, is `default-terminal`/`TERM` set correctly for color passthrough (see Terminal Multiplexers page)?
5. Only after all of the above — is the actual shell-side config (Starship TOML, `.p10k.zsh`, `PROMPT` string) correct?

The vast majority of "broken-looking prompt" reports resolve at step 1 or 2, which is why this diagnostic order front-loads them ahead of digging into shell configuration.

Reference.Glob Pattern Cheat Sheet:
## Standard globbing (identical in both shells, no options needed)

| Pattern | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `*` | Any string, including empty |
| `?` | Any single character |
| `[abc]` | Any one of `a`, `b`, `c` |
| `[a-z]` | Any character in range |
| `[!abc]` / `[^abc]` | Any character NOT in the set |

## Recursive globbing (`**`)

| Shell | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Bash | `shopt -s globstar` first |
| Zsh | Works by default, no option needed |

```bash
ls **/*.dart
```

## Extended patterns

| Meaning | Bash (`shopt -s extglob`) | Zsh (`setopt EXTENDED_GLOB`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero or one occurrence | `?(pattern)` | `(pattern)#` roughly, less commonly used directly |
| Zero or more occurrences | `*(pattern)` | `(pattern)#` |
| One or more occurrences | `+(pattern)` | `(pattern)##` |
| Exactly one of a set | `@(a\|b\|c)` | `(a\|b\|c)` |
| NOT matching pattern | `!(pattern)` | `^pattern` |
| Exclude a specific match from a broader match | not directly available | `pattern1~pattern2` |

```bash
# Bash — list everything except .md files
shopt -s extglob
ls !(*.md)

# Zsh — same result
setopt EXTENDED_GLOB
ls ^*.md
```

## Zsh-only: glob qualifiers (no Bash equivalent at all)

Appended in `(...)` after a pattern; see [Zsh In Depth → Options & Globbing](/bash-and-zsh/zsh-in-depth/options-and-globbing/) for full explanation.

| Qualifier | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `.` | Regular files only |
| `/` | Directories only |
| `@` | Symlinks only |
| `x` | Executable files |
| `L+100` | Larger than 100 blocks |
| `mh-24` | Modified within last 24 hours |
| `om[1,5]` | 5 most recently modified, sorted newest-first |
| `Om` | Sort by modification time, oldest first |

```zsh
ls *(.)            # regular files only
ls *(/)              # directories only
ls *(om[1,5])          # 5 newest files
```

## Case sensitivity and hidden files

| Behavior | Bash | Zsh |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Case-insensitive glob | `shopt -s nocaseglob` | `setopt NO_CASE_GLOB` |
| Match dotfiles with `*` | `shopt -s dotglob` | `setopt DOT_GLOB` (or prefix pattern with `.` explicitly, works either way) |
| Non-matching glob behavior | Passes through literally by default (`shopt -s nullglob` to expand to nothing instead) | Errors with "no matches found" by default (`setopt NULL_GLOB` to expand to nothing instead, matching Bash's opt-in behavior) — see the caveat on [Zsh In Depth → Options & Globbing](/bash-and-zsh/zsh-in-depth/options-and-globbing/) |

## Zsh-specific

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `PROMPT` / `PS1` | Primary prompt (interchangeable names) |
| `RPROMPT` | Right-aligned prompt segment |
| `HISTSIZE` | In-memory history entry limit |
| `SAVEHIST` | On-disk history entry limit (Zsh's equivalent of Bash's `HISTFILESIZE`) |
| `HISTFILE` | History file path (default `~/.zsh_history` if set explicitly — no default otherwise) |
| `KEYTIMEOUT` | Centiseconds to disambiguate `Esc` in vi-mode |
| `ZDOTDIR` | Overrides where Zsh looks for its dotfiles (`.zshrc` etc.), instead of `$HOME` |
| `path` (array) | Array form of `$PATH`, auto-synced; supports `typeset -U` for dedup |
| `vcs_info_msg_0_` | Populated by the `vcs_info` module for use in `PROMPT` |

## Startup-file variables (which file to check, per shell)

See [Getting Started → Startup Files](/bash-and-zsh/getting-started/startup-files/) for the full read-order explanation.

| Shell | Login files | Interactive (non-login) files |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bash | `/etc/profile`, then first of `~/.bash_profile` / `~/.bash_login` / `~/.profile` | `~/.bashrc` |
| Zsh | `/etc/zprofile`, `~/.zprofile` | `/etc/zshrc`, `~/.zshrc` (always, regardless of login status) |
